newsitem.title: HUNGARY: POPULAR HUNGARY PARTY CALLS FOR GOVERNMENT CHANGE.
newsitem.headline: POPULAR HUNGARY PARTY CALLS FOR GOVERNMENT CHANGE.

text.p: A congress of Hungary's popular opposition party Fidesz, held at the week-end as preparation for the 1998 elections, called for the replacement of the Socialist-Liberal government.

Fidesz said the country was sinking into deep corruption, living standards had fallen sharply while a small group was getting richer, and the government's policies still did not ensure sustainable economic growth.

"The theses approved by the congress may become the basis of the programme of a new civic government to be set up following the 1998 elections," vice president Tamas Deutsch told a news conference following the week-end party congress.
Fidesz is the only party in the Hungarian parliament, which has not been government member since the fall of the Communist regime in 1990.
The Socialist Party, which was founded on the ruins of Hungary's last ruling Communist party in 1990, came to power in 1994, after four years of a right-wing conservative government.

Fidesz and another opposition party, the Smallholders are running neck and neck in opinion polls ahead the senior government member Socialists, whose popularity slumped due to real wage cuts of about 15 percent in the past two years and a corruption scandal at the state privatisation agency in 1996.
"The governing left wing parties has weakened substantially and their support (from voters) has halved since the 1994 election," Fidesz vice president Janos Ader said.

Fidesz said a right wing government would crack down on corruption, narrow the gap between the rich and the poor and create sustainable economic growth by encouraging investments, cutting taxes and support small and medium size companies.
The government plans to boost the growth in gross domestic product to three percent this year and to four to five percent in 1998, up from one percent in 1996.

But the government's austerity programme launched in 1995 and including real wage cuts, has been suppressing growth and a rapid rise in current account and trade deficits, reversed by the programme, was likely to recur this year, Fidesz said.
Deutsch said a widening of trade deficit must be stopped, partly by encouraging those foreign direct investments which undertake to rely on Hungarian companies as suppliers.

He added that a Fidesz-led government would freeze the privatisation of such strategic companies as oil and gas company MOL, electricity company MVM, broadcaster Antenna Hungaria and air carrier Malev.

Fidesz agrees with the government that Hungary should join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and the European Union (EU), but the country must fight harder for its interests in future membership talks with the EU than it has done so far, Fidesz said.
Viktor Orban, 34-year-old president of Fidesz was absent from the congress due to an injury suffered at a soccer match, but the deputies reelected him with overwhelming majority.
